definition.text: A broad philosophy and social movement that seeks to protect living things, habitats and the wider environment.

facts.text: It advocates preserving, restoring and improving the natural environment, including systems such as the climate, and is often a movement to control pollution or protect biodiversity.
At its core it tries to balance people's relations with the natural systems they depend on so that all are sustainable.
The movement began as a response to rising smoke pollution during the Industrial Revolution; Britain's Alkali Acts of 1863 were the first large-scale modern environmental laws.
The 1972 UN Conference on the Human Environment in Stockholm, attended by 113 nations, led to the UN Environment Programme.
Its strands include free-market, evangelical and labour environmentalism and the conservation movement, and it gave rise to green parties.
Critics say early environmentalism reflected mostly white middle- and upper-class interests and overlooked indigenous communities and nearby low-income residents.
Every year more than 100 environmental activists are murdered worldwide.

definition.text: The view that free markets, property rights and tort law are the best tools for keeping the environment healthy and sustainable.

facts.text: It treats stewardship as natural and relies on individual and class-action lawsuits to drive out polluters.

definition.text: Trade unions' work to shape environmental policy, campaign on environmental issues and partner with environmental groups.

facts.text: Unions face a dilemma between the economic growth model and the global ecological crisis.
To promote green jobs, unions developed the idea of a just transition.

definition.text: Ideas and actions opposing environmentalism as a whole or particular environmental policies.

facts.text: It can take the form of an organized countermovement targeting climate science and environmental regulation.
Its actors may include workers in industries threatened by environmental policy and anti-environmentalist think tanks.

definition.text: The practice of protecting wild species and their habitats to keep wildlife populations healthy and restore natural ecosystems.

facts.text: Major threats include habitat destruction and fragmentation, overexploitation, poaching, pollution, climate change and illegal wildlife trade.
The IUCN estimates that over 42,100 assessed species are at risk of extinction, and a 2019 UN report put the figure for all species at a million.
More than 80% of the world's species live in forests, so deforestation is a major threat.
The illegal wildlife trade is estimated to be worth 7-23 billion, with around 100 million plants and animals traded a year.
In 1973 the US passed the Endangered Species Act, and CITES was agreed internationally to stop global trade in endangered wildlife.
Habitat conservation protects a whole habitat to protect the species in it, often preferable when many endangered species share it.
Monitoring populations lets managers track threatened species and test whether management works.

definition.text: The study of genetic factors that affect whether a species can be conserved.

facts.text: High genetic diversity improves survival because it gives more capacity to adapt to future change.
Low diversity brings inbreeding depression and drift, reducing adaptability and raising genetic problems.
By the early 1990s only 20-25 Florida panthers remained, highly inbred and suffering kinked tails, heart defects and low fertility.

definition.text: The non-living chemical and physical parts of the environment that affect living things and how ecosystems work.

facts.text: They include water, light, temperature, humidity, acidity, salinity, altitude, minerals, tides, dissolved oxygen and soil.
Humans can create or change them: fertilizers alter habitats and greenhouse gases change the ocean's pH.
Differences in them, such as water availability between rainforests and deserts, set limits on which species can live where and shape competition.
Factors such as salinity can give one species a competitive edge over another, creating pressure that leads to new species.
